questions.q: What pattern does this lesson's custom analytics rule detect?
options: Impossible travel — two successful sign-ins from the same account, from different countries, too close together to be real travel
A single failed sign-in attempt from any country
A user changing their own password
A scheduled analytics rule running more than once per day
questions.explain: Two successful sign-ins from different countries within an implausible time window is a classic sign of a stolen credential being used from two places at once.

questions.q: Why does the query filter on ResultType == "0" on both sides of the self-join?
options: Because failed sign-ins are always malicious
Because only a successful sign-in on each side is real evidence — a failed attempt from a second country proves nothing
Because ResultType has no effect on the query's results
Because KQL requires every join to filter on ResultType
questions.explain: Keeping only successful sign-ins (ResultType "0") on both sides ensures the comparison is between two real authentications, not a failed guess.

questions.q: In the scheduled analytics rule, what does the alert threshold control?
options: The color of the alert in the incident queue
How many matching results are required before the rule triggers an incident
How many hours of data the Log Analytics workspace retains
Which KQL operators are allowed in the query
questions.explain: The alert threshold decides how many results from the scheduled query are needed to fire — here, any result greater than zero.

questions.q: What does entity mapping accomplish for this rule's results?
options: It encrypts the query results before storage
It converts the KQL query into SQL automatically
It changes how often the query runs
It tags result columns like UserPrincipalName and IPAddress as real entities, so Sentinel can correlate this alert with other alerts touching the same account or IP
questions.explain: Entity mapping tells Sentinel which columns represent real entities (Account, IP address), which is what lets the investigation graph later link related alerts together.

questions.q: Why is this rule built as a self-join on SigninLogs rather than a simple filter on one row at a time?
options: Because SigninLogs cannot be filtered with a where clause
Because Sentinel requires every analytics rule to use a join
Because self-joins run faster than any other KQL operator
Because detecting impossible travel requires comparing one sign-in against other sign-ins from the same user, which a single-row filter can't do
questions.explain: A single row has no way to know about another sign-in from the same user — the self-join is what lets the query compare pairs of sign-ins against each other.
